context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome back to Education Joining the Dots. We are GL Assessment or GL Education, depending on where you are in the world, a renaissance company committed to delving into the most pressing topics in education and assessment. In this episode, we're exploring a topic that affects millions of children. We're delving into the critical issues surrounding speech, language and communication and how this impacts educational journeys for teachers and for their students. I'm your host, Georgina Cook, Education Specialist for Language and Literacy and former English lead across a multi-academy trust in the UK. Speech and Language UK report that one in five children are struggling with talking and understanding words. And the Oracy Commission point out that this means almost two million children in the UK were not at the expected level for language and communication by the end of reception. Two years on, we wanted to see if teachers thought speech and language problems were as widespread and if they were, what was causing them? Our recent loss for words report surveyed over a thousand UK teachers who revealed that up to 40% of students have speech and language issues, worsening over the past five years. Teachers blame reduced conversation at home, increased screen time and less reading. Speech and language barriers impact learning, well-being, behaviour and attendance. Teachers across the UK are struggling with these challenges every day, which are often misunderstood by the public and by parents. Joining me today is Rachel Simons, Reading Lead and Primary English Lead at Cabot Learning Federation. Join us as we uncover the realities of poor speech, language and communication skills in our schools and see what we can do to support every child's right to a successful education. Welcome, Rachel. Thank you so much for joining us today. Let's start by just introducing yourself, if that's all right, and what your role is at the moment. Of course. Thank you for inviting me. My name is Rachel Simons. I'm Reading Lead and Primary English Lead for Cabot Learning Federation. We're a large trust of 35 settings based in the southwest of England. I work as part of the school improvement team, which supports all of our school's adults and learners. So we have primary schools, secondaries, post-16, alternative and specialist provision, and we cater for children from the age of two to 19. Lovely. Thank you. Well, we really appreciate your time today. It sounds like you're a very busy lady with all of those children to look after. So in our recent Lost for Words report, teachers reported that up to 40% of students may have speech and language issues. And teachers believe that these skills have probably worsened since 2020 or since the pandemic. So I just wonder, Rachel, how prevalent these issues are across your multi-academy trust and what trends you've observed over the past few years. Absolutely. You know, we're certainly aware that there continues to be a growing number of speech and language needs apparent in early years and throughout other year groups in education. We know that the pandemic has impacted on this, but so too has the increasingly difficult financial situations that many parents find themselves in. Many parents working more than one job in order to put food on the table and they don't always have the time or the headspace to be able to narrate what they're doing, for example, in order to support their child's oracy. We also know that there's been a decline in the traditional childhood of playing, whether that's alone or with others too, and that more time is spent by children on screens instead of with each other, both indoors and outdoors and playing games. Given all of that as well, it's also apparent that as a profession, we're now more aware than ever before of speech and language needs. We're now more knowledgeable about them and we're certainly becoming more effective at supporting our young people to communicate better and to be

pending_qa.q: How have teachers' initial reservations about oracy development changed over time in the trust?
pending_qa.r: There were initial teacher reservations when first starting to develop oracy in schools. As teachers learned and developed knowledge around oracy, speech and language, and communication, they became skilled themselves. Reservations diminished quite rapidly because professional development upskilled teachers to guide and structure conversations, despite handing over lesson control to children.

pending_qa.q: How does oracy development support other areas of literacy like writing and reading?
pending_qa.r: Being able to talk through ideas before putting pen to paper is incredibly useful; 86% of staff at one secondary school believe oracy strategies supported students to complete higher quality extended pieces of writing. With reading, oracy makes it a sociable activity where pupils share what they learned, enjoyed, and what they agree or disagree with. Each person brings different perspectives based on their own experiences and knowledge, making shared views incredibly powerful and empowering for pupils of all ages.

pending_qa.q: What theoretical foundation supports the use of oracy in cognitive development?
pending_qa.r: Vygotsky's theories emphasize that communication tools are critical for cognitive development because they help shape the way individuals understand and interact with the world. Group activities and peer interactions enable learners to share ideas and perspectives, which enhance cognitive development and allow pupils to make sense of the world and articulate their feelings.
